bib.title: Electronic Commerce (Chapter 14)
bib.venue: book chapter, The Data Warehouse Toolkit (title and authors not printed on the chapter pages)

question: How do you model Web clickstream data dimensionally and integrate it with the rest of a retailer's warehouse, including channel profitability?
contributions: Clickstream-specific dimensions: page, event, session, referral
Fact tables at session, page-event and aggregate grain
Bus-matrix integration of the clickstream mart
Profitability fact table extending sales transactions across channels

results.claim: Session-grain clickstream fact table adds about 260 MB per day unindexed (52 bytes x 5 million rows).
results.setup: Hypothetical large site: 100M raw page events/day boil down to 5M sessions; 13 fields x 4 bytes

results.claim: Session-grain fact table: 94.9 GB unindexed per year.
results.quote: 260 MB x 365 = 94.9 GB of unindexed data

results.claim: Three years of session-grain data with indexing is estimated at about 600 GB.
results.setup: Session-grain table, 3 years plus indexing overhead; an estimate

results.claim: Page-event fact table: about 20 million meaningful page events per day after discarding GIF/JPEG image requests, from 100 million raw log events.
results.quote: 20 million meaningful page events per day

results.claim: Page-event fact table adds about 1.2 GB per day (20M rows x 60 bytes).
results.setup: 15 fields x 4 bytes = 60 bytes per row
results.quote: 20 million x 60 bytes = about 1.2 GB per day

results.claim: Page-event fact table: 438 GB per year before indexing.
results.quote: 365 x 1.2 GB = 438 GB per year, before indexing

results.claim: A session-grain aggregate (group by month, demographic type, entry page, session outcome) is almost certainly under 1 percent of the session fact table, so queries should run at least 100 times faster.
results.setup: Aggregate built from session-grain fact; asserted, no measurement
results.quote: almost certainly less than 1 percent of the original session-grained fact table

results.claim: Page dimension sizing: 100 bytes x 100,000 pages = 10 MB, about 40 MB with indexing (factor 3 as printed).
results.note: Arithmetic as printed: 10 MB x 3 = 30 MB, but text says about 40 MB (the same pattern holds for the other dimensions' totals).

results.claim: Event dimension: 40 bytes x 1,000 events, about 0.16 MB indexed.
Session dimension: 80 bytes x 10,000 combinations = 0.8 MB, about 3 MB with indexing.
Referral dimension: 100 bytes x 1 million rows = 100 MB, about 400 MB with indexing; hard to estimate without data.
A fully indexed 50-million-row customer table could occupy about 200 GB, a third of the session fact table.
Men enter a pseudonym on Internet forms 50 percent of the time and women 80 percent (stated as belief, no source).
results.setup: Name entered on an Internet form

limits: All sizing is a hypothetical worked example (100M raw events/day), not measured data.
Written for 2000-era Web tech (HTTP logs, cookies, proxies, XML pages); modern tracking (JS tags, event streams, consent) is not covered.
Authors concede session seconds cannot be known when the visitor leaves silently; extract assigns a nominal value.
Cost allocation for profitability is arbitrary where costs exist only as national yearly averages.
The 100x aggregate speedup is asserted, not measured.
practices: Give every visit a session ID generated by the operational application, not the Web server; the best tracker is a persistent cookie (p.282-283).
Choose the first clickstream fact grain as one row per completed session to keep volume manageable (p.292).
Keep the page-event fact table at the lowest practical grain; when too large, restrict time span or sample rather than aggregate away dimensions (p.295).
Do not create a page row per dynamic page instance; group dynamic pages by function and type (p.288).
Have Web designers assign content codes and attributes to every page and embed them in log fields (p.288-289).
Store universal (GMT) and local wall-clock date/time as two role-playing keys rather than computing time zones in queries (p.292-293).
Name non-equivalent measures differently (page seconds vs session seconds) so they are not added inappropriately (p.297).
Use a degenerate session ID on the page-event fact; keep the session dimension at class level, not per-session (p.296).
Put customer status labels in the session dimension rather than the customer dimension because they change quickly (p.290).
Build aggregate fact tables from shrunken conformed dimensions (month from day, demographic from customer) (p.298).
Do not attach a product-oriented causal dimension to the session-grain table because it is multivalued; put it at page-event grain (p.294).
Plan the data warehouse with a bus matrix: marts down, dimensions across; each X invites a conforming meeting; build first-level marts before consolidated ones (p.299).
Build the profitability mart on sales transaction grain (one product on a ticket) across all channels, not on sessions (p.301).
Store net revenue and gross profit physically if users reach the table directly; derive them in views otherwise (p.302).
Allocate Web site costs by pages per product, pages visited or Web purchases (p.303).
Use expiration dates and no-proxy/no-cache tags liberally to capture more events (p.285).

terms.definition: every page event recorded by each of the company's Web servers
the URL of the agent responsible for placing the link on the page
a unique identity tag for every visitor session, similar to a grocery store point-of-sale ticket ID
the number of seconds believed to elapse before the next page event
forward proxy belongs to an ISP and is outside your control; reverse proxy sits in front of your Web servers and is within your control
session ID: a unique identifier with no semantic content and no join to a dimension table
month table as a conformed subset of the calendar-day table; demographic as subset of customer
